analysis.one_liner: Toughens coal mine safety rules for evacuations, emergency communications, rescue teams, and penalties.
analysis.headline: This House mine-safety bill never got a vote and died in committee, but Congress passed its own version later in 2006 that became law.
analysis.plain_summary: Prompted by deadly coal mine disasters, this bill would have required every underground coal mine to have an approved emergency plan covering evacuation, breathable air supplies, and self-rescuer oxygen devices. It would have required wireless underground-to-surface communication and electronic tracking of trapped miners within three years, two certified mine rescue teams within an hour of every mine, and operator notification of accidents within 15 minutes. It also raised fines for safety violations, required stronger seals on abandoned mine areas, and funded research and training on mine safety technology.
analysis.who_benefits: Underground coal miners and their families gain the most: mandatory escape plans, cached oxygen devices, better communications, certified rescue teams nearby, and stiffer penalties on operators who ignore safety rules. Mine safety regulators also gain a larger trained workforce through new scholarships.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Underground coal miners and their families

how_it_helps.text: Each underground coal mine operator must adopt a written accident response plan, reviewed and approved by the Labor Department at least every six months, covering evacuation, rescue coordination, and maintenance of miners trapped underground [S2] [S3].

Plans must include emergency air supplies, caches of self-rescuer oxygen devices placed so no miner is more than a 30-minute walk from one, quarterly donning training, and flame-resistant lifelines in escapeways [S3].
Within three years, mines must implement post-accident wireless two-way communication between underground and the surface and electronic tracking of trapped persons [S2] [S3].
Operators must have an employee knowledgeable in emergency response on every shift and two certified mine rescue teams available within one hour of each mine [S2] [S3].

Operators must report a death or potentially fatal injury to the Labor Secretary within 15 minutes, with civil penalties of $5,000 to $60,000 for late notice and fines up to $220,000 for flagrant violations [S2] [S3].

The bill creates an Office of Mine Safety and Health within NIOSH to develop and speed the commercial availability of new mine safety technology, funds refuge chamber research, requires stricter standards for sealing abandoned mine areas, and establishes scholarships to train miners and mine safety inspectors [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators bear the cost: emergency equipment, wireless communication and tracking systems, rescue team staffing, higher fines for violations, and the administrative burden of approved, regularly reviewed emergency plans. Taxpayers fund the research, grants, and scholarship programs.

drawbacks.text: Operators argued compliance is costly: wireless underground communication, electronic tracking, extra rescue teams, and cached self-rescuers all require capital spending in an industry with thin margins, and some costs could surface as higher coal prices [S3].

The bill lets operators escape the wireless communication and tracking mandate if they claim it 'cannot reasonably be implemented' and offer an 'alternative' of approximately similar utility, giving operators room to argue their way out of the bill's most expensive requirement [S3].

The bill limits lawsuits against people and their employers who carry out mine rescue or recovery operations, except in cases of gross negligence, reckless, or illegal conduct — a shield that trades some legal recourse for encouraging rescue volunteers [S3].

Compliance disputes go to an expedited Labor Department administrative law judge process, which supporters called necessary speed but which adds a formal avenue for operators to contest required plan provisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are direct and measurable in lives: the disasters it responds to involved miners who could not communicate with the surface, ran out of breathable air, or waited too long for rescue teams. The costs fall on mine operators as equipment, staffing, and penalty exposure, with a real but bounded escape valve on the most expensive technology requirement. The liability shield for rescuers and the operator-friendly dispute process are concessions an honest supporter would acknowledge, but the core requirements — plans, air supplies, rescue teams, and 15-minute accident notification — are modest, targeted regulations on a demonstrably deadly workplace.

outcome.mechanism: The House never voted on it: after introduction it was referred to committee, then split between two subcommittees, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007 — though the Senate passed its own companion mine-safety bill that became law in June 2006.

narrative.text: Rep. Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV) introduced the bill on May 19, 2006, joined by West Virginia colleagues Nick Rahall and Alan Mollohan, months after the January 2006 disasters that killed coal miners [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced [S5].
On June 12, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Underground coal miners came out ahead in substance: a companion version passed the Senate and became law in mid-2006, imposing the emergency plans, rescue team requirements, communication mandates, and higher penalties. Coal mine operators avoided nothing — they took on those compliance costs under the enacted law — and this House bill's death in committee changed little in the end.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal miners, through the companion law

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and co-introduced by two Democrats, with cosponsors split evenly between parties (6 Democrats, 7 Republicans); its death in committee was not a recorded party-line vote but the absence of any vote at all.

industries.note: Operators would bear the cost of emergency plans, cached self-rescuers, wireless communication and tracking systems, rescue teams within an hour, 15-minute accident notification, and fines up to $220,000 for flagrant violations. Their compliance burden is precisely the safety protection miners gain, which is why their interest in weak requirements ran against miners' lives.

industries.industry: Mine safety equipment manufacturers and technology developers
industries.note: The bill mandates wireless communication, electronic tracking, and refuge alternatives, and creates a NIOSH office with grants to develop and speed the commercial availability of mine safety equipment — a market the bill itself notes is too small to attract ordinary commercial investment.
New Education Department scholarships and Labor Department safety-training grants would fund tuition and training programs, with special emphasis on workers in smaller mines.
